utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning Mr. Papic. Mr. Papic, yes. Good morning. Could you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Slokovic-Glumac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Slokovic-Glumac:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Papic.

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Good day to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please give us your particulars, where you were born, when and where do you live?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: My name is Zeljko Papic. I was born in Vitez in 1963 and I reside in Poculica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you live now?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: I now live in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you work in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: I worked at the Zenica waterworks, that is to say by the Krusica spring that gives drinking water to Zenica and Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you worked on this job, where did you go, where did you go to in the Lasva River Valley?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: From going from home to work, I would pass through Dubravica, the railway station, Rijeka, Krusica, and apart from Krusica, towards the mountain, because this spring that gave drinking water to the two towns I mentioned is about eight kilometres away from the actual village of Krusica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you often went to Krusica in '92, did you?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It was a kind of work duty for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you work there too?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During 1992 did the situation in Krusica change in any way?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes. As I went to Krusica, I realised that roadblocks were set up even because of the smallest of incidents, so it was very difficult for me to reach my place of work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were roadblocks set up at the main road or the road towards Krusica?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes, on the main road to and on the road leading to Krusica as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, could you look at this map and tell us which way you went and where is Poculica and where is Krusica and where was this waterworks. Could you please.

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: (Indicating) This is Krusica. This is the village. And the waterworks could have been somewhere up in the mountain by Zabrdje. So this is Rijeka and Poculica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the other side, on the other side of the road?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Krusica, Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The map is placed a bit awkwardly and all the witnesses are a bit confused when they see it.

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Well, the north is in a different direction. Vitez, Krusica and there are two roads that fork off here. The upper road and the lower road leading towards Krusica, towards Besici, and the upper part of the road leading to Bobasi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please show Poculica over here, below Ahmici. So you passed from Poculica to Dubravica?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Vitez, Rijeka, Krusica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were the roadblocks usually set up on that road in 1992 and who set them up?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: The roadblocks were most often put up at Rijeka. Some roadblocks were put up by Croats and about 100 metres away from that roadblock were Muslim roadblocks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any roadblocks at the entrance to Krusica?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there were. Precisely at this part of the upper road that I told you about, that leads to Bobasi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this place have a local name?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes. It's called Fatina Vodica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Would you please sit down again. So you said there was a problem of access. So how did you get to Krusica?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: In 1990, when the war broke out, on the 6th of April, 1992, we had special permits given by the MUP during a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The MUP is the police, right?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes. At that time it was actually called the SUP, and then after that they did not allow us to enter Muslim territory with those passes that we had. And we had to seek passes from the Territorial Defence that was at the school in Krusica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You sought permits from the Territorial Defence in Krusica or in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: In Krusica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the end of '92 and 1993, did the situation change? Were those permits, those passes sufficient?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes, permits were sufficient. However, under those conditions, namely, already in 1992, some time in September, the security guards at the waterworks actually belonged to the Territorial Defence, and every five days they sent in a new shift of 25 to 30 men to the waterworks building because we at the waterworks building had a big building in the shape of a hotel where our workers came for recreation purposes. And that is where they stayed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is to say that the members of the Territorial Defence stayed at that building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes. And I told you that the security guards already in September were actually Territorial Defence men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to work at the time, were you escorted by certain forces?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, from MUP, Vitez they took us to Krusica, the mentioned school where they actually had their barracks and their headquarters, and from the school to my workplace we were taken there by the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence at that time, did they have uniforms, insignia?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes. All the men who were guarding the waterworks building, all the Muslims wore camouflage uniforms and they had automatic and semiautomatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they have any kind of insignia on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Of course they did. I mentioned that they were the Territorial Defence and they had Territorial Defence insignia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any new buildings being built in Krusica?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Well, how couldn't I, when every other day I was in front of this school waiting to be transported to my workplace. And then I noticed changes, that there were lots of soldiers there and these were unknown soldiers. And at that time I noticed that in the upper part and the lower part of the school yard they started building small houses for the guards, and they also put wire all around the compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see a unit there at the time, at a given point in time were there groups of armed soldiers?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I noticed this. If the smallest incident occurred anywhere, there were more soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether they went to the frontline? Did you notice that?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes. They went to Cekrcici. They took buses. They wore uniforms and they had full military gear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In October were there any incidents in Krusica? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes, there were roadblocks. At that time I was at my workplace and for five days I could not leave the waterworks and I could not go home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you at the time?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: At the waterworks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when this was? At the end of October? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: I think it was the end of October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the HVO in Krusica, HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Four or five soldiers in Ribnjak, but I would just pass by. I was not in contact with them. And I couldn't have either, because I was being driven by a Territorial Defence vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what was in Ribnjak?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you pass by Lovac?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes, but as I went to work Lovac was about 250 or 300 metres away from the road I actually took. So I didn't really have access.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened in Poculica in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: In Poculica the situation was more or less normal, without any major incidents. Village guards were organised at the initiative of the local population because people feared for their property, for themselves. At the beginning this was done together with the Muslims, however, often they would leave us on our own quite often, regardless of what would happen, what kind of incident occurred. The very instant anything would happen, they would leave and go to Prnjavor. They would leave their own houses and go to Prnjavor. And Prnjavor is within the local community of Poculica. It has about 200 or 250 households, purely Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you belong to the village guards?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes, but rarely because of the work duty I had that everybody was aware of, and because of the responsibilities entailed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (No translation).

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes, I had a Czech Zbrojovka, a personal pistol with all the proper documents issued by the then SUP, and it was taken away from me when the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Poculica or in the other villages, you said that Prnjavor was the closest village to you and then Vrhovine, did you see over there, in 1992 or 1993 --

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes, I did see, because my house is just below the mosque and that is the only road leading to Prnjavor. Whenever the army would come in or go out, I could see it quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which army was this coming and going?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: That was the army that had Territorial Defence insignia, MOS insignia, insignia unknown to me, and I also saw soldiers who were wrapped up in something, and I couldn't understand the way they spoke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any places in Prnjavor where you noticed larger numbers of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes, because I know Prnjavor very well and these soldiers were stationed near Efendija's house. That's the largest house in the village, and it has a big yard. The house is near the road that I took when I was going to the shop. I could even notice that there was a kitchen there too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are trying to say an outdoor kitchen used for preparing meals for the military?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see these people wearing uniforms? Did they have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes. All of them wore uniforms and they had full military gear. When I say "full military gear," I am referring to automatic, semiautomatic weapons, RAP's, masks, and even knives that they had around -- that were hanging on their belts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see people equipped in this way in Poculica itself?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes, I did, because whenever the soldiers moved out of Prnjavor and whenever they went to any village, they had to pass through Poculica. And in Poculica I saw unknown soldiers too, soldiers unknown to me that is. And my neighbours who were armed and who wore uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they go to the frontline?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where to?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: They went to Cekrcici as well. That is what they said, at least.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could the witness please look at these aerial images.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D74/2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't understand what you said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take a look at these aerial photographs and tell us what they are. It is an aerial map of Poculica; is it not?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: This is an aerial map of Poculica, which is where the national structure, like Poculica proper, was in the ratio of 60 to 40. I say this approximately. That is to say 60 per cent were Croats of the population and 40 per cent were Muslims. The first half of the village was a purely Croatian part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the lowest part of the village?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes, the lower part of the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you show us on the map, on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: This is the lower part of the village (indicating), and the main road lies here. It is the Vjetrenica, Zenica main road. The first part of the village, as I say, was purely Croatian. The second part of the village from the elementary school maybe to the shop was mixed -- a mixed population. The area below the mosque, as I say, below the mosque, which is where my own house is situated, was predominantly inhabited by Muslims, and about 15 per cent were Croatian houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you point out your house to us and draw a circle around it.

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: (Indicating) Below the mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is the mosque? Would you point that out to us, please.

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: The mosque was somewhere here, and that is the road leading towards Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any trenches dug in the village, and if so, who dug them?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes, there were. In 1992 by the Catholic cemetery, Zvizda. The exact place is referred to as Gajevi and it is right by Poculica from which a hill which you can see Prnjavor from and part of Vrhovine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who dug these trenches?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: The trenches were dug by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any roadblocks in the village?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes, two. One manned by the Croats at Ogrev at the entrance to the village of Poculica, and the second roadblock was manned by the Muslims at Vjetrenica. The exact name of the location was Tabla. That's what this area was referred to. And this was controlled from the direction of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Poculica itself? Were there any major incidents in the course of 1993 before the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 15th of April, 1993, what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: On the 15th of April, 1993, in the morning, I had come back home from the nightshift, because I had gone to work on the 14th at 7.00 a.m. in the morning. And my work shift was 24 hours. And so I came at 7.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the night between the 14th and the 15th, were you in Krusica?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes, at the waterworks in Krusica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice anything unusual going on in Krusica?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes, I did. When I returned in passing, I noticed that there were more soldiers than usual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this frighten you?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Well, it didn't frighten me, but there was always some doubt as to why, who and so on, because there was general tension already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, in 1993, which unit had its headquarters in Krusica in the school building there?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: The 325th Mountain division, and I know some people who were in the command itself, and the person I know is Hakija Dzelilovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know him from before?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes, because he was in charge of the Plavac motel where I used to pop in as a guest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when he joined the BH army?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about the BH army, but I do know that in 1992 already, he was in the TO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you went home. Did you have any information as to a possible conflict on the 15th?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: No, I had no information of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened on the 16th in the morning?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: On the 16th of April, 1993 in the morning, it was around 5.30 or 6.00 a.m., I was awoken by strong explosions coming from the direction of Vitez. At that moment, where my house was situated, I was not able to ascertain exactly where the explosions came from, but strong explosions could be heard from the overall area around Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were in your own house?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes, I was in my house with my family, with my father, my mother and my grandmother, and she was 80 years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any shooting in Poculica?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: No. At that particular moment, in the early hours of the morning there was no shooting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Well, I did what I usually do. That is to say, as soon as the situation is tense, one becomes very disturbed. And there were planes circling, and there was a shelter. That is to say, there is a house with a basement dug into the ground, and it belongs to my uncle that house, and it is some 300 metres away from my own house. So with my family, because we were afraid that it would -- it could begin, that is to say that the shelling could begin, we moved into the shelter in this particular house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that because you were afraid of planes circling. What was that? You mentioned that. What was that? Do you mean in the war with Serbia or any other time?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes. What I mean was when the Serbian planes used to circle around us, and the basement was a sort of shelter in case of air attack, which would provide us with basic security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in that part of the village how many Croatian houses were there? What did you say?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: I said there were about 15 houses belonging to Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were the Croats from those houses?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: The Croats from those houses were situated predominantly in that particular basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anything happening or how long was it quiet in the village?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Well, up until 9.00 a.m. the situation was calm, but I was able to note my Muslim neighbours going out all the time with weapons, moving towards the mosque and Gajevi, which is the place that they dug trenches, which I mentioned a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the other part of Poculica was there any fighting going on, any war operations?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes. At 9.00 in the morning detonations could be heard in the lower part of Poculica, and this was inaccessible to me at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any fighting in the lower part of Poculica? Could you hear any fighting going on?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: All I could hear were the explosions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened next?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Sometime around noon, from the minaret, the tower of the mosque, the Hodza from Poculica called upon all the Croats to surrender themselves. "If you fail to surrender yourselves, we shall not be held responsible for you."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you give yourselves up?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: No, we were taken prisoner. When I say "taken prisoner," let me explain what I mean. That part of Poculica, that is to say from the shop towards the mosque and the houses below the mosque, that is to say the Croatian houses below the mosque, I was able to notice already at the time that armed soldiers were moving around in groups and that they were cleansing the Croatian houses. I was able to -- I saw this going on. They were clearing up the houses. I was not able to see what was on fire, but below the mosque itself, which is where the Croatian houses were located, there was a large cloud of smoke which means that something was already on fire. At that moment uniformed soldiers of the Muslim nationality, in groups of about five to six men, there were quite a few groups made up of five to six men, and they took control and surrounded the Croatian houses. Their tactics were first to throw devices which led to strong detonation. From these explosions you could hear glass being shattered and things being destroyed in the houses. As I already mentioned, the Croats from that part of the village and from these 15 houses were already located in the basement shelter of my uncle's house, so they came to the house very quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened in the house? Did the soldiers enter the house?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: As the basement of the house was on the -- in the lower part of the house, below ground level, and the door -- the front door to the house was up by the road, the soldiers drew close to the house, they had camouflage uniforms, they were armed, and the same system that I described a moment ago was repeated. They would throw these inflammatory devices and there would be detonations and explosions. We feared that something could happen. Perhaps they didn't even know that we were there. My uncle called out to them and said that there were only civilians in the basement. When I say "civilians," I mean that there were 75-year-old women, up to the age of 80, and there were children of between 5 and 15. There were women and men there as well and they were in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody have any weapons in the house?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: No, except for me. I had a pistol, which I have already described, and I had a permit issued by the SUP police station allowing me to carry the pistol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you shoot?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: No. They were able to ascertain that the barrel of the gun was quite clean and had not been used, and they did, in fact, look and check to see that that was so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were taken prisoner then. What happened to the other people?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: When they called out to us to leave the house, I saw five or six soldiers and they were painted with war colours, war paint. So some of the soldiers had black socks over their heads, but I recognised them by their voices because, as I say, I grew up with these men. When I called out to the man, he took the mask off his face, off his head, and at that moment I recognised him. He was Asim Bektas, and Muhamed Kulbegovic. They were soldiers who had their faces -- I did not know the two soldiers who had their faces uncovered, and I did not know what they were talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did they take you?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: The first man, Asim Bektas, ordered us to come out with our hands up in the air. Even the old women, the 80-year-old women had to do this, and unfortunately, the children as well. At that moment he said that Muhamed Kulbegovic was to take us in single file towards Prnjavor, but that the four women aged between 75 and 80, and some of them were even over 80, should remain there with my father in the basement where the conditions were terrible. It was a basement made of concrete and just earth on the ground, because it was not a proper shelter nor was it equipped properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your grandmother remained there?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes. Her name was Andza Papic. She was born in 1912.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to her?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: On the 21st she died in that basement. I asked the doctor to go and ascertain her death but he refused. A woman of that age was not able to survive that humidity and the cold in that basement, because there -- and I think that the cause of death was an influenza or something stronger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were the other civilians taken to, the children and the men -- and the women, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: They went together with me to Prnjavor, in a column. When they had gone to Prnjavor I saw that the shed was on fire belonging to Franjo Jurcevic, and that was the black cloud of smoke that I had seen previously from the shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you show the Court please where Prnjavor was located and where the house is that you were put up? Would you use the ELMO to point it out to us, please?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: This is the part going towards Prnjavor and Vrhovine, whereas the centre is at the crossroads of the road -- the junction from Prnjavor to Vrhovine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is that?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: It's behind my house, in the direction of this road. Somewhere in this locality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the houses opposite your house, whose houses are those?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Below my house are the Muslim houses belonging to a family called Sivro, that is their surname, and Bektas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you point out where the centre in Prnjavor is? Can we see it on this map?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: I can only see a section of the road, and the centre -- the community centre was somewhere at the junction, which means somewhere around here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is almost joined to Poculica?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was put up in that community centre?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: May I also mention that while we were marching in single file towards Prnjavor by Efendija's house, and I already mentioned his house, were the private houses belonging to Nasid. This private house belonged to Nasid, and that's where they began to separate the women and children, and they took them towards the basement of his house, whereas us -- they took us men towards the community centre in Prnjavor, the community centre which was where dances were held before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was in the community centre? How many men were there?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Well, when I arrived at the community centre I found several of my neighbours there already, but as there was a mop-up operation in the village of Poculica, they would bring men in from the village and hold them prisoner there. There were about 30 men there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were the women? Where was your mother and the others?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: I've already said that by Efendija's house they separated them from us and that they were put up in the basements of the private houses there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they taken prisoner or were they allowed to move around freely?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: They were not allowed to move around freely, they were prisoners. At least my mother was according to what she told me, because I wasn't able to see it because I was already a prisoner myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the -- how long did you spend in the community centre?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Well, on the 17th we were taken to do trench digging, and a group of people in the centre, that is to say there were two large windows in the community centre which were facing -- which faced Poculica, and as there were just fields, arable land between Poculica and Prnjavor, it is this lateral part -- may I point it out on the map?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: So this is the community centre, and in the direction of Poculica there were two big windows from which we could clearly see Poculica itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you see happening in Poculica? Were houses on fire there?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes. I saw Stipan Ramljak's house in flames. I also saw women and children moving around and moving from the Croatian houses in Poculica, and they were taking away Croatian property, and livestock and everything that belonged to the Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were they taking this livestock?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: They were taking them in the direction of Prnjavor. And my Croat neighbours who were prisoners in the community centre could clearly see, at that moment, their own cows or horses. They could see them being led off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was anything else happening in the village?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes. On that particular day, the 17th, and I did not know that at the time, but Bozo Kristo was killed in front of the post office. And they were killing pigs in the village. Not a single pig was left alive, they were all killed. I was able to see this for myself, because together with a group of prisoners I went to dig -- to bury those pigs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said that you were taken trench digging, where did you go to dig trenches and who took you there? Who took you off to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: We went trench digging to Sivrino Selo. However, at the entrance to Sivrino Selo, myself and two other men were set aside to dig a trench in Suhi Hrastovi. That was a place which lies between Dubravica and Sahadinove Kuce.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took you away, the military or the police?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: It depended. The army and the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were most of the people from the community centre taken away?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes. The next day when we returned in the evening, that is to say in the morning the next day a group of 20 people were taken off to do work and to dig trenches at Sivrino Selo. According to the words of a soldier who had come to the community centre and who distributed the soldiers and said who would be going, he said that they tried not to have a father and son go together or two brothers going together, because if anything were to happen, to have at least one family member alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they say where they were taking the men and what type of work they were supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes. They said they were taken to Sivrino Selo to do trench digging, and a portion of these people should serve as a human shield towards the cemetery at Sivrino Selo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the women in the community centre with you?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: No, they were not women from Poculica, but on the 22nd -- in the night between the 22nd and the 23rd, in the evening hours of the 22nd, that is to say, at 6.00 p.m., some women were brought in, five women, in fact, from the village of Putkovici. And when they came to the community centre when, they were brought there, we were told that they had been brought from Preocica and that they were to be exchanged the next morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Putkovici is a Croatian village, is it the not?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes, it is a purely Croatian village which had already been cleared up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 23rd in the morning, what happened then, tell me, at the community centre?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Sometime in the morning, it was early, I think it was around 9.00 in the morning, I did not have a watch, and this was the third day that we were there at the community centre, and they put wooden boards on the windows because they realised we could see what they were doing in the village. So it was already dark in there. And on the 23rd and on the 24th, 1993, I heard something strange going on outside, and very often -- and very soon this was confirmed. And gunfire could be heard and then we could smell gunpowder. There was this terrible stench all over. Then there was blood all over. I saw that I was wounded in the arm, hand, in the back, and I turned to -- and in the neck too. Then I turned around and I saw Perica Papic, my cousin, and he had been hit and was already dead. He was born in 1962. And behind him his maternal uncle, Jozo Vidovic, born in 1945, and Ivo Vidovic, born in 1938. In addition to myself, amongst the prisoners there were three other men that were wounded, and these three women who were supposed to be exchanged, but they did not succeed in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did the shooting and how?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Above the door there was a glass pane -- there used to be a glass pane, but then there were short bursts of gunfire that broke it, and this went through the door and through this small part of the window, because there were two of them by the door. On the right-hand side towards that part of the wall it is only these two men who were there that remained unwounded. Everybody else was wounded to a larger or a lesser extent, and I already mentioned who was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Pero Papic was killed, but you also mentioned Jozo Vidovic and Ivo Vidovic. Were they killed.

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I said that I saw them dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they take you to the hospital then?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Not that very moment, because after the door was opened, the door was broken down, and Safet Sivro barged in. At that time he was the commander of that particular branch of the BiH Army, Prnjavor, Poculica and Vrhovine. He asked who had done this. No one said a word to him. Before the shooting started, when I mentioned that something was going on outside, I recognised the voice of Bektas at the door, behind the door. Not the Asim I already mentioned. This one had a nickname of Lepina and he was working at the Zenica mine and he was over 45 years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he in military uniform?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: During the first two days he wore civilian clothes, but he was armed. He had an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you transferred to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: We were transferred to the hospital only around 11.00, and before that an orderly came, his last name was Haseljic. I know this young man very well, but I only know his surname. I didn't know his first name. He started bandaging people's wounds. He tried to stop the bleeding of those who had already been bleeding for quite some time, and he only had plain bandages to use.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they took you to the hospital, right?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they did. At that moment they took us to the hospital, towards Zenica. But before we reached the hospital, they took us to the house of corrections, and from the ambulance I only realised that I was within the house of corrections compound and I saw that something strange was going on. Again, people were squabbling, as if in the marketplace, whether they should leave us there or whether they should take us to the hospital. And after a brief quarrel amongst them, we were taken to the hospital in Crkvica, to the traumology ward.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay there in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: We stayed in the hospital until the 13th of May, 1993 until 6.30 p.m. That is when I was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you heavily wounded?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes. After I left the hospital in Crkvica, I continued my treatment in the hospital in Bila.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you return to Poculica?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: No, never, because Muslim refugees are living in Croat houses there and 40 per cent of the houses were burned down. Over 40 Croat houses in Poculica were burned. Practically 70 per cent of this Croatian part in the lower part of the village was burnt down, so reconstruction hasn't started yet. But I already went to Poculica twice, but I did not go to my own home. I went to the cemetery. Our cemetery called Zvizda to visit our dead. It's one of the older Croat cemeteries. As we came to the cemetery, we realised that all the tombstones were broken and that the chapel was set fire to and that the crosses were all over the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not go to see your house, what condition it was in, and the house that you lived in?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: My mother says that it was considerably damaged, but refugees are living in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, tell me, who buried your grandmother when she died in that basement?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Well, the already mentioned Safet Sivro came on the 21st in the morning and he said that my grandmother had died, and that I could bury her straightaway in the garden of my uncle's house. However, since we grew up together, since we were actually friends too, we would go out in the evening together and we were very close. And he allowed me to bury her at the Zvizda cemetery that I mentioned a few minutes ago. He actually did allow me to do so. The late Perica Papic went with me, Franjo Jurcevic and Josip Papic too, the four of us. We took her to the cemetery and that is where we dug her grave and we were accompanied by two guards. And as we were labouring, the cemetery is about 15 metres away from Franjo's house, there was no drinking water available. However, we were not allowed to -- even to walk that way, let alone have a drink of water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's just one thing that we omitted. What were the conditions like at this centre? Did you have anything to eat or drink?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: What they gave us, and they hardly gave us a thing, and I shall explain this. On the first day I remember well, some time during the night we got some kind of rice that had already gone sour. As regards conditions, I already mentioned that the floor was concrete and the first two or three days we had only a few blankets, which was not sufficient for 30 people. There was a concrete floor and our main point was not to lie on the concrete itself. So we put the blankets down and then we would cover ourselves with the jackets and the other clothes we had. May I just finish my thought? Very often we were provoked by soldiers in uniform and one day a soldier in uniform walked into the hall where we prisoners were and he started beating everyone in sight. He lined us up and we had to repeat after him Muslim prayers. But he never found it loud enough. So we had to do it louder and louder. And people could hear this all the way to Poculica. We did all of this out of fear, because we were afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other Croats who were imprisoned, do you know when they were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: My parents say that they were exchanged on the 1st of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my last question. The people you saw while you managed to see through these windows, what was going on in the village; were these people you knew, people you did not know, and were they armed or unarmed?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: All of them armed, and I knew quite a few of them and I didn't know even more of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these Muslim soldiers, and with what kind of insignia?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: As far as I could see, most of them had MOS insignia. That is to say the Muslim armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you. I have concluded my questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we take a break, may I ask whether other Defence counsel are willing to cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I only have one question and the other defence attorneys do not wish to question this witness. I don't know whether I should do it now or after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, if it is a short question, right away, yes. Cross-examined by Mr. Pavkovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, my name is Petar Pavkovic. I am Defence counsel. I have just one question for you. You said that you noticed, around the school in Krusica, certain changes, that something was going on there. You said that you saw them building some kind of small house, and that they were putting up a fence around this yard.

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what they used this for?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: This was used for military purposes. This was used for the guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you sure that it was only used by the guards or --

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: No, I mentioned here that there were these little houses to be used by guards, and the building that was built underneath the school made up of different elements. It was not accessible to me. So there was this new building built just below the school, and the little houses that I saw, as I pointed out, in the lower part and in the upper part of the school yard within the fence were meant for military purposes, for carrying out military duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not know whether they brought some Croats there, whether they locked them up or something? Did you know anything of that nature?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: No. At that point I did not know anything of this nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take a 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: I apologise. I didn't want to interrupt the Court, but I have two questions to ask the witness, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course. So if you don't mind, Mr. Blaxill, do you mind waiting for a few minutes. Counsel Susak, please go ahead. Cross-examined by Mr. Susak:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, my name is Luko Susak and I am Defence counsel for Drago Josipovic. You said you were in Crkvice in the hospital there. Where is Crkvice located?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: It's a suburb of Zenica, within the frameworks of the city of Zenica itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you were taken to the hospital there, did you receive any document saying you were a prisoner -- saying you were arrested? Were documents of this kind given to anybody else?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: No, only what the Red Cross recorded. Perhaps on the second day of our arrest, on the 17th or 18th, somewhere thereabouts, but no documents certifying to our arrest existed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were not in the Zenica house of correction before that, or were you taken there?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: No, I was not taken to the prison itself, but when I went to my company I passed by the KP centre, that is to say the house of correction, and the head office of my company was located in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was held prisoner in the penitentiary?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: No, I don't, but a lot of Croats came to Vitez and they said that they were -- they spent a month in the penitentiary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know any other place where Croats were held prisoner in Zenica itself?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Well, rumour had it that they were held in the basement of the music school. And the music school is situated near the former bank of Sarajevo, the Prnjavor bank of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if there were any Mujahedins?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes, I even saw them. I saw them in Poculica and in Prnjavor by Efendija's house. I have already mentioned Efendija's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know they were Mujahedins?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Well, they didn't hide the fact. They had the scarves that they wore. They did not understand Serbo-Croatian and they were dark skinned, compared to us that is. But, as I was born there, I knew, at least by sight, all the locals, including Poculica and Prnjavor, from Vrhovine and Vjetrenica and further afield as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they instill fear in the Croats?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what way did they do this?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Well, they made us afraid of them because when they would pass by our houses, they would very frequently express their type of greeting, and other forms of religious exclamations. So that part I understood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the school of music.

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned the music school because there were Croats who were detained there and ones that I knew, and who came to Vitez to be exchanged. And one of the people there was Anto Vrvilo, who complained of his injuries and said he was beaten up every day and he lost a lot of weight, 20 kilogrammes. And he is still an unwell man today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said there were two prisons, one located in the music school and one in the penitentiary?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes, I said that I heard this from others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who detained the Croats in the music school and who detained the Croats in the penitentiary building?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Well, according to what I heard, the music school was the MOS prison, that is belonging to the Muslim armed forces, whereas the KP penitentiary building was where the members of the army took people, and they were visited by the Red Cross. Whereas those detained in the music school were inaccessible to anybody. Nobody was allowed to meet them, to visit them, except for the ones that beat them up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Red Cross have access to the detainees in the music school?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: I don't know. So I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned MOS. Will you tell us what MOS means?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: MOS is an abbreviation for the Muslim armed forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who composed these Muslim armed forces?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: They were predominantly the extremists from amongst the MOS Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry, Counsel Susak. You said you would ask two questions, and specific questions, I imagined. But you are now moving to general questions. We have already heard a lot about MOS and so on. Do you need to ask all these questions? If you could be as concise as possible, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will try and be as brief as possible. But this was my introduction to my brief questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that these people were detained in the music school and the penitentiary. Could you tell us how the exchange was effected, who organised the exchange, and where did it take place?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the Croats of Zenica were exchanged for Muslims from Vitez?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Well, yes, there were exchanges.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You already told us when. Will you tell us who performed these exchanges, prisoner exchanges, and where, if you know that.

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: I am not aware of that, but certain localities were pinpointed. I don't know exactly. But I do know that the exchange was done via the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who participated on the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: I don't know. When I myself was exchanged, I was not able to move. And when I was brought to the Suhi Hrastovi locality, there was just the driver, his name was Botic, and there was a doctor present, a doctor working in our outpatient department.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examined by Mr. Blaxill:

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, I'm obliged to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Witness. My name is Michael Blaxill. I'm one of the Prosecutors working on this particular case. I do have a few questions for you but I hope mercifully to be as brief as I possibly can. I believe in late 1992 there was an ongoing conflict, was there not, with Serb forces not very far from the Lasva Valley area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: That's correct, in the Vlasic area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And I believe in Kruscica (pronounced phonetically) -- Kruscica, I'm sorry, I think that's a better pronunciation, you saw a build-up of buildings and enclosure of what was perhaps -- was it a TO military centre? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes. It belonged to TO but I didn't say buildings, I said that a circle had been made around the school, and huts were being built on the upper and lower side of the courtyard near the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the enhancement of the installation was taking place against the backdrop of an ongoing conflict with the Serbs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: I see no reason for that because the Serbs were far away from us, and I said that the Serbs were located further up from Turbe. So I see no reason for these huts to be built up around the school in Kruscica. As far as the fighting with the Serbs is concerned, there was no reason for this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you also say, do you not, that you saw an increased traffic of troops coming into the area and then going out again, an increased traffic of troops going through; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: I don't think I used the word "traffic," but I said that in the morning when I passed by the school in Kruscica that I saw larger numbers of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time, am I right in saying that there were no outbreaks of violence or difficulty between the Croat and the Muslim populations in the village of Poculica? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: I don't know what period you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This would be, let us say, the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: The beginning of 1993, up until the 16th of April, in fact, yes, up until the beginning of the conflict. On the 16th of April there were no excesses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you say you returned home at 07.00 on the 15th of April. Did you do anything in particular that day in terms of your duties with the village guard or not?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: No. I was on holiday doing work in the field, and I went to bed in the evening, up until the moment in the morning between 5.30 and 6.00 a.m. when I was woken by detonations from the direction of Vitez. I did not have any assignments or anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I interpret you correctly, sir, you clearly felt that there were no impending threats and no potential outbreak of a conflict in terms of the atmosphere in Poculica on the 15th?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you say you heard detonations from the vicinity -- or the direction, I'm sorry, of Vitez on the early morning of the 16th of April. That is correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe you quoted the time as somewhere around 05.30 to 6.00 in the morning, is that so?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: That's what I said, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think -- what -- sorry. I'll ask this differently. What, in fact, did you do when you woke and heard these explosions? Did you report for duty somewhere or take any particular action?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: The only action that I took was to save my family and to place them in a shelter, and so I went together with my family to the shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you -- you placed your family in the shelter. Did you join your family in that shelter or did you go elsewhere in the village?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: No, I didn't go anywhere else. I was non-stop near them, within five metres. I was always together with them. I just went outside the house for a moment but nothing else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe you described the shelter as a basement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes. It was the basement of the house that was being -- that was still under construction. It had a roof but nothing much else, and the basement was three metres by four, dug into the ground, and the house itself was a three-storey building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the basement have any kind of aperture to the outside air or was it completely underground? In other words, could you see out of the building at all?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: The door was dug into the building and there was a small window. That is to say, there was just an ordinary opening. There was no window, it was just a small opening one by one metre, for example, in the basement, and it faced the Veseli Drug cafe and the Muslim houses owned by the Sivro family. That was the surname, Sivro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm going to go back just briefly to one point I recall you mentioning. You referred to aeroplanes circling. Did you actually see aeroplanes early that morning circling over the valley?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't mean that morning, I meant that the Serbian planes which had circled in 1992 around Princip in the town of Vitez. I didn't mean that they were circling on that particular morning. Apart from the detonations that I heard from the direction of Vitez, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe -- pardon me. You say that up until about 09.00 that morning, certainly there was no sound of any fighting or detonations or anything like that within Poculica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: That's correct. Apart from the Muslim army, which could be noticed bearing weapons and in uniforms was moving in the direction of the mosque and the people digging trenches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And presumably did you observe these Muslim soldiers through the one metre by one metre aperture in this basement, is that correct, or is that something you heard later?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: No, I saw them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You remained, it seems, in that shelter until about 12.00 or after 12.00 hours that day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: That is correct, yes. Until the Hodza from the minaret of the mosque called to us to surrender, and when the clearing up began and when they began to encircle the Croatian houses, that is to say, the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your references to whatever had occurred in Poculica as such, those references are to detonations you heard whilst you were in the basement of the building; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said a moment ago. I said that I was able to go out of the basement from the lower part of the house so that I would leave for brief moments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So throughout -- but throughout that particular period when you heard these detonations, for the most part you could not identify who was firing at who or from where, would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: I was not able to identify them, no. I just heard detonations from the direction of Vitez, but I did not know what was happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm referring now, sir, though to the detonations you say you heard elsewhere in Poculica. But you were, in fact, in a basement at the time of hearing those; that is correct?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes, below the house. And I also heard those detonations, as I have already said, between 5.30 and 6.00 a.m. when I was on my way to the shelter. I also said that my uncle's house was approximately 3 to 400 metres away from my own house, and that's how I heard them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at approximately 12.30 that day, you were effectively captured by some soldiers you identified as Muslims forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: That's right. And I recognised some of them. Some of that group that circled our house and that called to us to surrender, but only after they heard cries from my relation, Perica who called out to them to tell them not to shoot because they were civilians there. And we left the basement and then saw that two of these solders had black socks over their heads. Three of them had war paint, black war paint on their face, and the third one was covered up. I didn't know him and he didn't understand me either, and he was sort of translating what was going on to some of the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were then taken, I believe, to the community centre by those troops, and you and your family and others were placed in custody in a concrete basement; is that correct? That's in Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: That is correct, except for the four women, including my grandmother who died in the basement. At that particular moment, on orders from Asim Bektas, they stayed in the basement, whereas all the rest of us went in column, single file up to the basement. And I also said that by Efendija's house they separated the women from the men -- that is to say the women and children, I apologise, the women and children were separated from the men and we men were taken to the community centre in Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you were in custody at the community centre, I believe that you say that you were taken on the 17th of April to go trench digging. I believe that's correct. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. And I was taken to dig the pigs that they had killed in the village as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was on the same day, sir?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you then remained, I believe, in that location until the 24th of April; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were kept in custody at that location until, I believe, the 24th of April; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: I was kept in custody in the community centre up until the 23rd of April when I was injured and when the people were killed that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a particular person in that connection. I think a nickname of Lepina or something, is that right, a guard?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: That's right. I said Asim Bektas, nicknamed Lepina, who worked in the mine in Zenica, and he was about 45 years of age. And you should not be surprised by the fact that I mentioned the same name and surname of the man that took me into custody and guarded me, who has the same name and surname, in fact, because in Prnjavor, there are 30 or maybe more houses with the same surname, and very often the names are the same as well, but they are usually referred to by their nicknames. So the one at the door was nicknamed Lepina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe you said you heard a voice at -- just before that appalling shooting incident involving that room; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: That's right. I heard and recognised the voice as being that of Lepina and Zejdin Tatarevic. That is to say, people who were seen all the time and whom I contacted with all the time. So it wasn't difficult to recognise them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say that after this incident, I believe the commander came in -- was it the commander who came in?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes. And I also mentioned that Safet Sivro was the commander of Poculica, the Muslim part, and Prnjavor was purely Muslim and Vrhovine was purely Muslim inhabited.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his reaction when he came in and saw what had happened?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Well, it was one of panic, I would say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe you said he demanded to find out who had done it; is that correct? He asked who had done it?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: That's what he said, and went outside and didn't return.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to ask you a couple more questions about timing if I may. I know it's an element of repetition, but perhaps I can be forgiven just for emphasis, but if I get the scenario correctly for the 16th of April, you heard detonations in the Vitez direction at about 05.30 or 06.00. You heard other detonations at around 09.00 when you were in the basement in the shelter, and the only contact you had then with the military was when you were seized at about 12.30 in the early afternoon. Is that roughly the correct timing of the day?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: That is correct. It is true I heard detonations from 6.30 (sic) to 6.00 a.m. It is also correct that I saw detonations in the lower part of Poculica at around 9.00 a.m., and contacts with the Muslim army I had at around 12.00, after the Hodza had appealed from the minaret to us to surrender. Which means that on that morning I was in contact with the people who had held me in custody, which was the Muslim armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Just for the record, I think there was a mistranslation. Clearly in the answer he said from -- probably he said from 5.30 to 6.00, whereas in the transcript we see 6.30 to 6.00, which is illogical. So we should put it straight.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. Obliged to you for that, Mr. President. In fact, Your Honours, I have concluded cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Slokovic-Glumac? Re-examined by Ms. Slokovic-Glumac:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Papic, during your testimony you mentioned a few names. You mentioned those two Asim Bektas and Muhamed Kulbegovic?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Muhamed, Asim Bektas, Lepina and Zejdin Tatarevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those are the people you recognised at that point; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how they behaved before that? What kind of people were they in relation to the Croats?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Well, in relation to the Croats, until the elections they would say hello to us and vice versa. But I would single out Asim Bektas, this MOS commander who took me prisoner, from the elections onwards. One could notice that he was a bit more of an extremist than the other Muslims, because meetings were often held between the Muslims and the Croats in Poculica and various issues were being resolved in this way in order to keep the war -- to keep peace and order. And I remember that he said once, "I know what I'm fighting for, and I'm fighting in the name of Allah and I'm fighting a holy war, Jihad."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that you were engaged in the village guards only from time to time?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: That's right. I said from time to time, because I already had this work duty and I carried it out regularly. And due to my job description, I also had to work during the night as well. So 24 hours of my work were there. I had to work at night too. So I really couldn't work round the clock, that is to say, go on guard and also go to work, but it would happen that I would go out for guard duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said, during the cross-examination, that you noticed that the army was going towards the mosque and towards the area where the trenches were.

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: That's exactly what I said. And my neighbours at that, in full military gear. I even noticed a neighbour of mine carrying an M-53, a heavy machine gun, and he did not even say hello, he simply speeded by me and they left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So why were they going there? They did go out to dig trenches? Because the transcript said that they went out there to dig trenches, which is probably a mistake.

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: No. I said that already in 1992 they had dug trenches in the area of Gajevi, and I did not mention that they went out to dig trenches on that day at all, because why would they be digging trenches in full military gear?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in Kruscica you actually had barracks -- a school that was transformed into barracks. Did you notice any changes in that barracks in 1993? In addition to building these little houses, did you notice anything else, any other changes?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Well, there were all changes in terms of the military setup.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what sense the military setup?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Well, very often they would often go to Kujevac, which is in the mountains and there are big meadows there. I used to go that way to work too, and that is where they had training or something, I don't know, but I would see them go up there in uniform and with weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you notice them going out for training or for reviews, military exercises? Did you see anything of that nature?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Not in Kruscica but in Poculica, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this last question, when you talked about these detonations, these first detonations in the morning, you said that they came from the direction of Vitez. The other detonations that you heard later, where were they coming from, or, rather, where were these detonations taking place, can you tell?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: I can, and I said that I heard these other detonations around 9.00 a.m. in the lower part of Poculica populated by Croats. I also heard gunfire from Gajevi, and after that detonation in the lower part of Poculica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did this detonation go on in the lower part of Poculica? While you were still in the village could you hear detonations then too?

utterances.speaker: Zeljko Papic
utterances.text: Yes, yes, every now and then. But I already said that around noon I was taken away, so --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. No further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. No questions from the Court. Mr. Papic, thank you for testifying in court. You may now be released. Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I think we could -- we can't afford to waste 25 minutes. I wonder whether we could bring in the next witness, Mr. Vidovic. It's 25 minutes. It's a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any protective measures for the next witness? No. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am sorry. Could I please tender into evidence this Defence Exhibit D75/2 -- 4/2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No objection. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vidovic. Could you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Please be seated. Counsel Radovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Radovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you please introduce yourself to the Court. Your name is?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: My name is Rudo Vidovic, the son of Jozo and Milka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please give us your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: I was born on the 5th of November, 1958 in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where exactly? Where were you exactly born?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: I was born in Pirici, the local community of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where do you live now?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: Now I live in Vitez, in the street Kralja Petra Kresimira Street, No. 52.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, what do you do now? What post do you hold?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: I now work in the telecommunications centre and I am the director of the telecommunications centre of Central Bosnia with its head office in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, what have you finished by way of schooling?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: I have a higher education. I am called a communications engineer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is this post-secondary education imply?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: Two-and-a-half years of schooling after secondary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you attend secondary school?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: I attended secondary school in Zenica. It was an electrotechnical school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, tell me, you were born in Pirici. Please describe to the Court the position of Pirici as related to the central part of Ahmici, so-to-speak.

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: Yes, I was born in Pirici. And my family home is, until this very day, above the school in Ahmici, on the left-hand side of the road that leads to Ahmici. It is about 800 metres away from the main road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
