utterances.text: Tell us, this house of yours, is it in the exclusively Croatian area or is it in a mixed neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: My family house is practically the first one in the Croatian part, that is to say Zume, which is a neighbourhood with a Croatian majority. That is on one side. On the other side there is exclusively Muslims, that is to say the Bosniak people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you went to secondary school in Zenica, did you live at home or did you live in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: I lived at home and I travelled to Zenica by bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your relationship like with your Muslim neighbours, as well as that of your family? I am talking about the period while you were still at home, that is to say before you finished secondary school and before you went onto Sarajevo to continue your education?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: Well, the members of my family and I, throughout this period, had a good relationship with our Muslim neighbours. I can say it was more than good, as a matter of fact. These were good neighbourly relations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please describe these good neighbourly relations to us.

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: We visited one another, we would have coffee together, and we would help one another with the farm work. Also, we did certain things for one another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you graduated in 1979, and I imagine that after graduation you did your military service in the JNA, and then what did you do after your JNA service? Where did you find a job?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: Yes. I came from the JNA in December, 1980 and I first started working at the post office in Travnik on the 15th of January, 1981, and I was a trainee, an engineer trainee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you continue to live in Pirici at that time?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. All that time I lived in Pirici with my parents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, after you returned from the army, were you a member of a political organisation, for example, of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia? I am again using abbreviations that only we are aware of.

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, while you lived with your parents in Pirici, that is to say from 1980 until 1984, were you actively involved in social political affairs in Pirici or were you only a passive member of the League of Communists?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: Well, at that time, from 1975 onwards until 1983, with the exception of '79, when I was in Sarajevo, and '80, when I was in the army, I was actively involved in the work of the local community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did this active work consist of?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: At that time an asphalt road was being built. This was between the main road and the village of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your activity precisely?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: I was a member of the organising committee for building this road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, this local community, what are the villages that it consisted of?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: The local community of Ahmici consisted of the villages of Ahmici, Pirici and Nadioci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these exclusively Croatian villages or were they both Croatian and Muslim villages, or were they mixed villages?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: They were mixed villages with the exception of upper Ahmici and upper Pirici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who lived in upper Ahmici and upper Pirici?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: In upper Ahmici and upper Pirici, that is where Muslims lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, where did the Muslims of Ahmici meet their religious needs? Did they have a mosque in Ahmici or did they have to leave Ahmici in order to reach a mosque where they could pray?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: In the early years, that is to say from 1970 until 1980, in upper Ahmici there was a house that they called the Mejtef. They carried out their religious rites.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, did that building have a minaret or not?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: No. No. It was a small, old house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that old house ever get a minaret or not?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: No. Never. Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Please continue, and I apologise for having interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: From 1980 an initiative was launched to build a new mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who launched this initiative?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: The local population of Gornja Ahmici. And this mosque was built in Gornja Ahmici, I think in 1985 or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that mosque have a minaret?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That one didn't have a minaret?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Never?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there another mosque?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: In 1989 my parents' next door neighbour, Hazim Ahmic, built a private mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, generally speaking, was Ahmici generally well-known for having this private mosque or was it simply unusual? Did people talk about it a lot for that reason or was it customary?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: I think that that was the first private mosque that was built at that time. It was precisely in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We all know, according to photographs, what this mosque, which had been destroyed, looked like, but what was the attitude of the Croats? That's what I am interested in. Because this is in the lower part of the village where there were quite a few Croats. What was the attitude they took in relation to the building of this mosque, and perhaps in passing you could also mention the role of your late father in the building of this mosque?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: All of us know about the disagreement between the initiative of Gornja Ahmici and Donja Ahmici, as far as the building of the mosque was concerned. Namely, the villagers of Donja Ahmici did not agree with this location of the mosque that was built in the upper part. And, in a way, they supported Hazim to build this mosque in Donja Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: Well, probably because of their financial interest, because --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They didn't have to pay anything?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: They didn't have to pay anything. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: However, at that time it was impossible to build a private mosque without the approval of neighbours, notably those of different ethnicity. Without having received their consent in writing, that is. My late father and a few more neighbours gave a written statement that they would not mind having such a religious building, namely, a mosque built. This written statement was sufficient for obtaining the necessary technical documents. And the mosque was built. It was completed with a minaret in 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, your late father and this person, Hazim Ahmic, were they in personal contact?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: Well, yes, they were. They were good friends.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there an inaugural ceremony?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: Yes, there was an inaugural ceremony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were Croats present there?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: Yes, they were. Croats were there too. And perhaps even more Croats were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your late father there?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: My father did not attend the inauguration because he died two-and-a-half years before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But then you told me that your late father, sometime before his death, was in touch with Hazim Ahmic, and could you tell us what this was all about?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: Yes. In June, 1989, the foundation was laid for this mosque and there was a ceremony dedicated to this, and Hazim and his wife, Celbija, went to the Hodza after that and there was a big party to see them off. At this party, in addition to many other Croat neighbours, was my father. A month after that he died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, that is to say that Croats gave their consent in writing for the building of this mosque, and did Hazim do the Croats some kind of favour, I mean in a material, financial sense?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: Yes. At that time the Topolsko cemetery became too small.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This Topolsko cemetery, is that the cemetery where the roadblock was on the 20th of October? Is that that cemetery?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We just want to have a clear situation as to where this cemetery actually is. Yes, please proceed. It's a Catholic cemetery, is it?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So then what did Hazim Ahmic do in this connection?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: The cemetery, the cemetery borders Hazim Ahmic's land, 60 per cent of it as a matter of fact, and Hazim gave part of his own land to expand the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he give it away for free or did he charge a price or was it a very low price?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: He did charge a price, but it was a very low price. And also he offered even more land at a very low price, because at that time a church was supposed to be built by this cemetery too. And, of course, it never was built, nor did its construction ever begin. Well, I can only imagine for what reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the reason?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: I don't know why the construction never started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, while you were in secondary school and while you went to university, was there a cultural society in Vitez that was involved in folk dancing?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there was. This cultural and arts society of the SPS of Vitez, and there was a folklore section and there was also a group that was involved in music. And I was a member too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long were you a member of this section?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: This was in 1982 and 1993 (sic).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is to say that you stopped this activity in 1983; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, in view of your position in Pirici, did you as a secondary school student and as a young boy, did you know a person called Zoran Kupreskic, and then in passing you can also tell us about Mirjan Kupreskic, whether you know him too?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: Yes, but of course we grew up together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us approximately how far away your house is from his house, as the crow flies, from your house to their house -- to their houses? Well, I mean, you don't have to give us the exact figure in terms of metres, but you are just giving us an approximation. But as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: Rudo Vidovic
utterances.text: Four hundred and fifty metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Now I am moving onto a question where I shall mention another neighbour and his son, and I think that that part should be in closed session. Since we have only a half a minute left, I believe that there is no point in drawing the blinds now and everything. So if you agree, I believe that I may conclude at this point for today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Could I interrupt for a second. I believe lines 117 double dot 16 and 18, there has been a translation problem. The first question, I think, was to do with folk music, 1982 and 1993, and then it said stop the activity in 1983. So I think it was just that "1993" is a mistranslation. It should be 1983 at that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: One of those lines has a mistranslation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Blaxill. All right. We adjourn until tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
